intended_object: The canonical R-linear isomorphism R⟨X_σ⟩/aᵏR⟨X_σ⟩ ≅ (R/aᵏ)[X_σ]. Here R⟨X_σ⟩ is the ring of power series whose coefficients tend to 0 (a)-adically, a is a regular element, and the map reduces every coefficient modulo aᵏ. Inferred from the docstring, the module documentation and the companion `_mk` simp lemma.
explanation:
The body is the first isomorphism theorem applied to the reduction map `linearAdicReduction`. That map is R-linear and surjective onto `MvPolynomial σ (R ⧸ (a)^k)`, and it sends a restricted series to the polynomial of its coefficients modulo (a)ᵏ. The library proves that its kernel is the submodule (a)ᵏ • ⊤, which is aᵏ·R⟨X⟩. The construction combines `Submodule.quotEquivOfEq` with `LinearMap.quotKerEquivOfSurjective`. The simp lemma `principalLinearQuotientEquiv_mk` confirms that it sends the class of f to its reduction, so this is the canonical map, not an arbitrary isomorphism.

`adicallyRestrictedSubring I` is the set of series whose image modulo Iᵏ is a polynomial for every k. That is exactly the condition that the coefficients tend to 0 I-adically, so the domain is the restricted power series ring. The R-algebra structure is the expected one, given by constant series.

The regularity hypothesis on a is what the kernel computation needs. It lets you cancel aᵏ to produce a quotient series that is still restricted. Without it the kernel can be larger than aᵏR⟨X⟩: for example, when σ →₀ ℕ is uncountable and a coefficient lies in ⋂ (aⁿ) but is not aᵏ times an element of ⋂ (aⁿ). So the hypothesis is a natural condition for the statement, not an arbitrary restriction.

Mathlib has no restricted multivariate power series ring for an adic ideal and no such isomorphism, so nothing in Mathlib generalizes this construction. The ring R is an arbitrary commutative ring and σ an arbitrary index type, which is the natural generality.
